title: Car Seat Safety: Mistakes, Expiration Dates, and Care
summary: Avoid the most common car seat mistakes—loose installs, LATCH errors, expired seats—with tips from a Child Passenger Safety Technician
body_markdown:
Nearly half of all car seats are installed incorrectly according to the[National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA)](https://www.nhtsa.gov/press-releases/nhtsa-highlights-importance-car-seats-and-child-passenger-safety) . Considering how critical a role they play in child safety, that is not a statistic to be taken lightly.


The basics of installing a car seat correctly are not difficult to learn and parents should feel confident that they will be able to install a car seat properly on their own. However, there are plenty of common car seat installation mistakes that are worth pointing out. The plethora of different models, shapes, sizes and configurations can overwhelm even seasoned parents and caregivers, let alone first-timers, and just like many other aspects of raising children, there is no formal training, and we figure things out as we go.


That's where Child Passenger Safety Technicians (CPSTs) are here to help! We spend our days immersed in all things 'car seat' so parents don't have to. This guide aims to help parents avoid common car seat mistakes, how to best use a car seat, and how to know when it's due for replacement. Simply, we want to ensure parents feel empowered to install and use car seats correctly.


- **What's the Right Car Seat for My Child's Age and Size?**
- **What Are the Most Common Car Seat Installation Mistakes?**
- **What Mistakes Do Parents Make When Securing a Child in the Harness?**
- **When Do Car Seats Expire, and Why?**
- **How Do I Clean a Car Seat Without Compromising Safety?**
- **Frequently Asked Questions**
- **Bottom Line**


Question Short answer


**What's the #1 car seat installation mistake?** A loose fit—the seat shouldn't move more than 1 inch front to back and side to side at the belt path


**When do car seats expire?** Typically 6–10 years from the date of manufacture, not the purchase date


**Can I machine-wash the harness straps?** No—spot-clean only with mild soap and water


**Can I use LATCH and the seat belt together?** No—both are equally safe, but use only one method at a time


## What's the Right Car Seat for My Child's Age and Size?


This is among the most common questions CPSTs are asked—and we always answer it with more questions. There are three key things parents should ask to establish whether a car seat is right for your child: does it fit the child? Does it fit the vehicle? And is it installed correctly every time?


The very youngest children—newborns until sometimes as old as 18 months—should always sit in a rear-facing child seat. While convertible seats and all-in-ones can serve this purpose, most parents will opt for infant seats, which are designed to easily transition between use in a car or on a stroller.


Infant seats typically have a weight limit of around 30 lbs. and a height limit of 30-32 inches, and there should be a distance of at least one inch between the child's head and the top of the headrest when they're sitting in the seat. It's recommended to use this type of car seat until your child maxes out the height or weight limits.


When your child outgrows an infant seat, they're ready for a forward-facing harness car seat, which may be a convertible or all-in-one seat. All convertible car seats can accommodate the rear-facing infant seat stage, but can also be positioned forward-facing once the child has grown. All-in-one Car Seats can transition from harness to booster and grow with children from around age two up to eight-to-10-year-olds. If in doubt of what stage is right for you, always check the manufacturer's guidelines for the seat, which should clearly state the exact height and weight limits and requirements.


Booster seats are designed to raise a child to a height at which a standard car seatbelt secures them across their hips and shoulders—not their belly or neck. There are high-back boosters and backless boosters, that can accommodate children from at least 4 years old and up to ages eight to 12.


Our article How to Choose the Right Car Seat goes explains the different types of seats in even more detail.


Stage Orientation Typical limits Key transition cue


**Infant seat** Rear-facing only Up to ~30 lbs. / 30–32 inch (varies by model) Child's head is ~1 inch from the top of the headrest


**Convertible seat** Rear-facing → forward-facing Grows with the child; varies widely by model Experts recommend staying rear-facing as long as the seat allows


**All-in-one** Rear-facing → forward-facing → booster Grows with the child; varies widely by model Maximize the weight and height limits for each stage


**Booster seat** Forward-facing, belt-positioning Used once the child outgrows the forward-facing harness Seat belt sits across hips and shoulder, not stomach or neck


## What Are the Most Common Car Seat Installation Mistakes?


1.


Loose fitting seats are one of the most common car seat installation mistakes. Seat bases typically have a tightening strap that's pulled to secure them in place, and one way you can check whether your car seat is securely installed is by using the inch test.


The car seat 'inch test' is a simple way to check whether a car seat is installed tightly enough. Grab the seat at the belt path with one hand and try to move it side to side or front to back. If it moves less than one inch, it's properly secured. If it moves more than an inch in either direction, reinstall for a tighter fit.


2.


Another mistake is that people often believe they're being extra safe by using both LATCH and seat belt connections when installing a car seat, but that's not true. Both LATCH and seat belt installations are equally safe, but they should not be used simultaneously. The installation method is up to the parent, but there is a federal standard that limits LATCH connections to 65 lbs. for both the seat and the child combined. Beyond that 65 lbs. combined weight limit, car seats must be installed only with seat belts.


3.


An incorrect recline angle is also common, and this can be especially problematic for infants who need a more reclined position to keep their airways open. Many car seats feature a level that indicates correct and incorrect recline angles, and you can see it in action in our video Car Seats: How to with the Gurus.


4.


Forgetting about the top tether is yet another common car seat mistake. It's an adjustable strap with a metal hook that connects the top of a forward-facing car seat to the vehicle's anchor point to reduce forward movement in the event of a crash. The anchor point is usually found on the back of the seat, on the rear shelf, on the ceiling, or on the floor; check the vehicle's manual if it's not obvious.


Top tethers should always be used with forward-facing car seats, because they significantly reduce a child's forward head movement in a crash.


## What Mistakes Do Parents Make When Securing a Child in the Harness?


1.


Leaving the harness too loose is one of the most common mistakes made when securing a child. There is a 'pinch test' that can help avoid it. After buckling and tightening the harness, try to pinch the webbing of the belt at the child's shoulder, making sure you are pinching along the length of the webbing, not the width. If you can't pinch any excess material, that means the harness is snug enough; if you can, it needs to be tighter.


2.


Child Passenger Safety Technicians recommend following a specific order when securing a child in the seat. First, secure the crotch buckle snugly around the child's hips, then connect the chest clip. The chest clip should always be at armpit level—never up near the child's neck or down by their stomach.


3.


Another common mistake—and easy to miss—has nothing to do with technique and entirely down to clothing. Bulky coats, jackets, blankets and other chunky garments can affect the fit of the harness. Compressible material and bulky clothing can create a false sense of snugness. It's an easy fix though, simply keep blankets and coats on the outside of the harness and consider warming the car before placing your baby in it.


## When Do Car Seats Expire, and Why?


Car seats do expire. The average lifespan of a car seat can vary between six and 10 years from when the seat was built (not when it was sold), depending on the product manufacturer and the seat's usage frequency. The car seat expiration date can usually be found molded or printed on the seat shell, on a label, or in the owner's manual.


Child safety car seats have expiration dates primarily to ensure that the latest and greatest lifesaving technology is available in the market. Moreover, expiration dates take car seats out of circulation after years of use (and abuse!) to make sure their performance is not affected by wear and tear.


CPSTs generally advise against buying used car seats, because they don't come with the same standards and guarantees as new ones and it can be difficult to determine a seat's condition and whether it's been involved in a crash. Parents should only opt for a used seat if it comes from someone they know, trust and can verify the seat was not involved in an accident. Anyone considering a second-hand car seat should check the expiry date to see if it's still within its usable life, and visit the NHTSA website to confirm it was[not part of a recall](https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls) .


## How Do I Clean a Car Seat Without Compromising Safety?


One absolute certainty is that kids make a mess. The harness straps, the cover, and the padding will need to be cleaned at some stage, but it's important to clean up the mess with care to keep the seat safe and operating correctly.


Harness straps should never be machine-washed, soaked, or cleaned with bleach, vinegar, or harsh chemicals. They should only ever be spot cleaned using mild soap and water.


There's a critical reason for this: the harness webbing is designed to stretch slightly in a crash, and this is engineered into the fibers. Harsh washing or chemicals can degrade that strength, which is why simple and gentle cleaning techniques are the way to go.


When it comes to the seat cover and padding, the best advice is to check the manual. These can often be machine-washed on a gentle cycle, but they might have to be hand-washed or spot-cleaned, depending on the product. They should always be left to air dry, because machine drying can shrink or warp the padding and labels.


Component Do Don't


**Harness straps** Spot-clean with mild soap and water; air dry Machine wash, soak/submerge, or use bleach, vinegar, or other harsh chemicals


**Cover / padding** Check the manual; most hand- or gentle-cycle wash; air dry Machine dry (can shrink or warp padding/labels)


**Shell / buckle** Wipe down with water; swish buckle in plain water if needed Use abrasive scrubbers or solvent-based cleaners on the shell


## Frequently Asked Questions


### How do I know if my car seat is installed tightly enough?


Use the car seat inch test. Grab the seat at the belt path and try to move it side to side or front to back. If it moves less than one inch, it's properly secured.


### What is the pinch test?


The car seat pinch test is a great way to tell whether a harness has been fitted correctly. Once you've buckled and tightened it, try to pinch the webbing of the shoulder belt at the child's shoulder. Pinch in the direction of the webbing, not across it. If you can't grasp any excess material, then the harness is tight enough.


### Can I use both LATCH and the seat belt at the same time?


No. LATCH and seat belt installations are equally safe but should not be used simultaneously.


### How do I find my car seat's expiration date?


The seat's expiration date should be molded or printed into the seat shell, listed on a label, or published in the manual.


### Can I machine-wash the harness straps?


That's a hard no. The harness straps should only ever be hand-washed with mild soap and water, because machine-washing can compromise the harness webbing's performance in a crash.


## The Bottom Line


Car seat mistakes are easy to make, but they're also easy to correct. It's completely understandable that parents or caregivers would find themselves looking at a car seat and scratching their heads, as it can be brand new territory.
